items.q: Did living to ~79 give us more youth?
items.a: **Mostly no.** The jump from a historical adult life around 50 to ~79 added **old-age years**. Dopamine, reaction time, physique, and cognition all peak earlier. Treat his ~79/21 value split as a sketch, not a measured law.

items.q: What does the late-life end often look like in this video?
items.a: Not a peaceful bonus 30. He cites a 2004 Japan list (**hospital deaths**, cancer / stroke / heart; 'old age' ~2.3%) and four grandparents who died in hospital. Use as mood, not epidemiology.

items.q: What changes if you assume you die at 50?
items.a: Long compounding looks insane. At 17 skip the master's; at 37 stop optimizing the channel and go to Tibet. An **80-year** clock picks late-game heroes: 复读, IB, then a 50-year-old 董秘 seat.

items.q: Why compare an 80-year life to a long 王者荣耀 match?
items.a: If the match is long, you pick a **late-game** hero and sit under tower. That is rational for max money. It is less rational if the extra 30 years are the low-value, high-illness ones.

items.q: What does Becker add to 'time is money'?
items.a: Every hour has a **wage-equivalent** price. A ¥35 movie that takes two hours at ¥100/hour costs **¥235**. School costs tuition **and** the wage you did not earn.

items.q: Does maxing money or maxing leisure win?
items.a: **Neither pole.** All-grind → ¥23.36M and zero leisure, cheaper late experience. No work → all the hours and no money for travel or a house. The score is lived experience, not the pile.

items.q: Why can later money fail to buy the same joy?
items.a: Windows close. A skipped graduation trip has no cohort later. A childhood yo-yo is not the same at 37. **回忆股息**: a good year keeps paying in later recall.
**No.** Picasso, Joan of Arc, James Dean, 手冢治虫 are not the answer, but the vivid parts were not money. Do the age-bound things (and travel with living parents) before the window shuts.
